questions.stem: In 1520 smallpox spread through Tenochtitlan during the Spanish conquest of the Aztec (Mexica) Empire. Why did the disease have such a devastating effect?
options: Indigenous peoples of the Americas had no previous exposure and so no immunity to it
The Spanish had developed a vaccine and gave it only to their own soldiers and allies
The disease had been brought to the city by traders arriving from Ming China
The Mexica refused to treat the sick because their religion forbade any medicine
questions.explanation: Smallpox, measles and influenza had never reached the Americas, so whole populations lacked immunity and died in huge numbers. This weakened resistance to conquest. Vaccination was not developed until the 1790s.

questions.stem: In 1680 the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, led by Popé, rose against Spanish rule and drove the Spanish out of the region for twelve years. Which cause best explains the revolt?
options: Forced labour, drought and famine, and Spanish suppression of Pueblo religion
Spanish plans to grant the Pueblo full citizenship and seats on the Council of the Indies
A Pueblo alliance with the British, who promised to take New Mexico for themselves
The withdrawal of all Spanish missionaries, which left the Pueblo without trade goods
questions.explanation: Demands for labour and tribute, years of drought and hunger, and the punishment of Pueblo religious leaders combined to provoke a coordinated revolt. It shows how imperial control could be overturned, at least for a time, by Indigenous resistance.

questions.stem: In 1683 the Ottoman army failed to capture Vienna, and by the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) the empire gave up most of Hungary. What did these events mark?
options: An alliance between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs against the Russian tsars
The end of Ottoman expansion into Central Europe and the start of territorial losses
The Ottoman conquest of the Habsburg Empire and the move of its capital to Vienna
The beginning of Ottoman rule over the Balkans and the city of Constantinople
questions.explanation: Karlowitz was the first treaty in which the Ottomans gave up large territories to European powers, showing that the balance of power had shifted. The Ottomans had ruled the Balkans and Constantinople for centuries before this.

questions.stem: In the decades before 1644 the Ming faced famines, rebellions, debts from costly wars including one in Korea, and a falling supply of silver. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Internal and external pressures combined to weaken the dynasty before its fall in 1644
The Ming fell only because the Qing had a stronger army, whatever the conditions inside China
The Ming fell because Zheng He's voyages had emptied the treasury in the previous decade
The Ming were at the height of their power and fell because of one unexpected battle
questions.explanation: Climate-driven harvest failures, peasant revolt, costly wars, factional struggles at court and disruption to silver imports all weakened the state, allowing rebels and then the Manchus to take power. Zheng He's voyages had ended two centuries earlier.

questions.stem: Aurangzeb, the last of the great Mughal emperors, spent decades fighting in the Deccan. What was the main consequence of these campaigns?
options: They forced the British East India Company to leave India for good
They united the Mughals and Marathas against the Persian ruler Nadir Shah
They drained the treasury while the Marathas continued to resist Mughal rule
They ended all opposition and left the empire stronger than at any time before
questions.explanation: The long Deccan wars against the Marathas and southern sultanates were enormously costly and never fully successful. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, succession struggles and regional powers broke up central authority.

questions.stem: In 1773–1775 a Cossack named Yemelyan Pugachev led a huge rebellion against Catherine the Great by claiming to be:
options: Tsar Peter III, Catherine's murdered husband
the Ottoman sultan's chosen governor of Kazan
the heir of the Ming emperors of China
a prophet sent by the Orthodox patriarch
questions.explanation: Pugachev claimed to be Peter III, who had been overthrown and killed in 1762, and won support from serfs, Cossacks and non-Russian peoples angered by serfdom and taxes. The rebellion was crushed and Pugachev executed.

questions.stem: Spain governed its American empire through two great viceroyalties, which were:
options: Granada and Castile
New Spain and Peru
Brazil and the Philippines
Florida and the Caribbean
questions.explanation: The Viceroyalty of New Spain, based in Mexico City, and the Viceroyalty of Peru, based in Lima, were each headed by a viceroy appointed by the Crown. Brazil was Portuguese.

questions.stem: In Spanish America, the encomienda system gave a colonist:
options: the right to export silver directly to Asia without paying any tax to the Crown
the labour and tribute of a group of Indigenous people, with a duty to convert them
ownership of a large estate that he could sell freely to any other colonist he chose
a seat on the Council of the Indies in Spain for himself and his descendants
questions.explanation: Encomenderos received the labour and tribute of Indigenous communities and were supposed to protect them and teach Christianity. In practice the system led to great abuse, which the Crown tried to limit with the New Laws of 1542.

questions.stem: The Spanish adapted the Inca mita, a system of rotating labour service, in order to:
options: supply workers for the silver mines at Potosí
train Indigenous men as soldiers for Spain
build churches in every village of the Andes
send Indigenous people to work in Seville
questions.explanation: Viceroy Toledo reorganised the mita in the 1570s to force Andean communities to send men to the mines of Potosí, where conditions, including mercury poisoning, were deadly. The silver financed the Spanish Empire.

questions.stem: The Portuguese cartaz system in the Indian Ocean required Asian merchant ships to:
options: carry Portuguese missionaries on every voyage
sail only in convoys led by Portuguese warships
buy a Portuguese pass or risk being seized at sea
pay a yearly tribute in gold to the Mughal emperor
questions.explanation: Using naval power from bases such as Goa and Hormuz, the Portuguese sold licences to trade, controlling sea lanes rather than territory. Ships without a cartaz could be captured. This was a method of imperial control based on force at sea.

questions.stem: After its victory at Plassey in 1757, the British East India Company gained the diwani of Bengal in 1765. What did this mean?
options: The Company won the right to collect Bengal's land revenue, making it a ruling power
The Company had to pay Bengal's land revenue to the Mughal emperor each year
The Company gave up trade in India in return for a share of the Mughal customs duties
The Company handed Bengal over to the British Crown, which ruled it directly
questions.explanation: The Mughal emperor granted the Company the diwani, the right to collect revenue, turning a trading company into the government of a rich province. Direct Crown rule in India came much later, in 1858.

questions.stem: Under the Canton system, introduced by the Qing in 1757, European merchants were:
options: allowed to trade in any Chinese port and travel freely in the empire
banned from buying tea and silk, which the Qing kept for themselves
required to live in Beijing under the supervision of the emperor
restricted to trading at Guangzhou through licensed Chinese merchants
questions.explanation: The Qing limited Western trade to Guangzhou (Canton), where it passed through the Cohong guild of merchants, and kept foreigners out of the interior. British frustration with these limits led to the Macartney mission of 1793.

questions.stem: The phrase ‘God, gold and glory’ is often used to sum up the motives of Spanish and Portuguese conquerors. ‘God’ refers to the aim of:
options: finding the Garden of Eden in the Americas
building cathedrals to rival those of Rome
proving the pope's claim to rule the world
converting Indigenous peoples to Christianity
questions.explanation: Spreading Catholicism was a genuine motive and a justification for conquest, alongside the search for wealth and personal fame. Missionary orders such as the Franciscans, Dominicans and Jesuits followed the conquerors.

questions.stem: Bartolomé de las Casas, a Dominican friar who had once held an encomienda, became a fierce critic of Spanish treatment of Indigenous peoples. At the Valladolid debate of 1550–1551 he argued against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda that:
options: the encomienda should be extended to every Indigenous community in New Spain
Indigenous peoples were fully rational human beings who should not be enslaved
Indigenous peoples were natural slaves, as Aristotle had taught about some peoples
the Spanish should withdraw from the Americas and leave the colonies to Portugal
questions.explanation: Las Casas defended the humanity and rights of Indigenous peoples, while Sepúlveda used Aristotle's idea of natural slavery to justify conquest. The debate shows competing motives within the empire itself, though neither side was declared the winner.

questions.stem: In New France, French officials, fur traders and Jesuit missionaries all depended on alliances with Indigenous nations such as the Wendat (Huron). Why did French traders need these alliances?
options: Indigenous hunters and trade networks supplied the beaver furs the trade needed
Indigenous nations controlled the French navy that carried the furs back to Europe
Indigenous leaders appointed the French governor at Quebec each year
Indigenous farmers grew the sugar that New France exported to France
questions.explanation: The fur trade depended on Indigenous hunters, guides and trade routes, so the French made military and trade alliances with nations such as the Wendat and Algonquin. Sugar came from France's Caribbean colonies, not New France.

questions.stem: Merchants of the Dutch East India Company and Jesuit missionaries both travelled to Asia. How did their motives differ most?
options: Both refused any contact with Asian rulers and traded only with each other
The Company sought trade profits for shareholders; the Jesuits sought converts
The Company sought converts to Calvinism; the Jesuits sought profits for the pope
Both sought only to conquer territory and settle European farmers on it
questions.explanation: The VOC was a profit-seeking company answerable to shareholders, and in Japan it kept its trading post partly by not preaching. The Jesuits aimed to spread Catholicism. Both still had to negotiate with Asian rulers.

questions.stem: The ‘Columbian Exchange’ refers to:
options: the bank Columbus founded in Seville to fund later voyages across the Atlantic
the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and elsewhere
the trade agreement Columbus signed with the Ming emperor after reaching China
the exchange of prisoners agreed between Spain and Portugal under the Treaty of Tordesillas
questions.explanation: The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term for the movement of crops, livestock, people and disease after 1492. Columbus never reached China.

questions.stem: Which list contains only crops that spread from the Americas to the rest of the world through the Columbian Exchange?
options: Potatoes, wheat, tea and bananas
Maize, barley, oranges and olives
Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and cacao
Wheat, sugar cane, rice and coffee
questions.explanation: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, chillies and tobacco originated in the Americas. Wheat, sugar cane, rice, coffee, tea, bananas, barley, oranges and olives all came from Afro-Eurasia.

questions.stem: Which animal brought by Europeans most changed the lives of Indigenous peoples of the North American plains?
options: The bison
The horse
The llama
The turkey
questions.explanation: Horses brought by the Spanish spread north and transformed hunting, travel and warfare for plains peoples such as the Comanche and Lakota. Llamas, turkeys and bison were already native to the Americas.

questions.stem: In the ‘triangular trade’ of the Atlantic, ships carried manufactured goods from Europe to West Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, and then:
options: spices and tea from the Indian Ocean around Africa to Lisbon
furs and timber from Russia across the Baltic to Amsterdam
sugar, tobacco and cotton from the plantations back to Europe
silver and silk from Manila across the Pacific to Acapulco
questions.explanation: Plantation crops grown by enslaved labour returned to Europe, completing the triangle. The Manila galleons crossed the Pacific, a different route linking Spanish America and Asia.

questions.stem: Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean relied heavily on enslaved Africans. Which reason best explains why planters turned to the transatlantic slave trade?
options: Sugar could only be grown by workers who had already farmed sugar cane in their homeland
Indigenous populations had collapsed, and sugar needed very large forces of labour
European law banned planters from using any Indigenous or European workers on sugar estates
African rulers demanded that every European ship carry captives as a condition of trade
questions.explanation: Sugar was extremely labour-intensive, and Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean and coastal Brazil had died in vast numbers. Planters bought enslaved Africans instead, building economies on brutal forced labour.

questions.stem: The journey of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic was known as the:
options: Northwest Passage
Silk Road
Spice Route
Middle Passage
questions.explanation: The Middle Passage was the middle leg of the triangular trade, in which captives were packed into ships in terrible conditions and many died. The Northwest Passage was a sought-after sea route around North America.

questions.stem: Huge quantities of American silver entered Spain in the sixteenth century, yet the Spanish Crown declared bankruptcy several times. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Spain gave the silver to the Ottomans as tribute to keep peace in the Mediterranean
Costly wars across Europe consumed the silver, and rising prices hurt Spanish industry
The silver was all stolen by English pirates before it could reach the port of Seville
The Crown refused to accept silver and demanded that all taxes be paid in gold
questions.explanation: Silver paid for Habsburg wars in the Netherlands, Italy and against the Ottomans and England, and much flowed out to foreign bankers and suppliers. Inflation, the ‘price revolution’, made Spanish goods less competitive. Pirates took only a small share.

questions.stem: In 1621 the Dutch East India Company conquered the Banda Islands, killing or deporting most of the inhabitants and bringing in enslaved workers. The Company's aim was to:
options: protect Bandanese traders from Portuguese raids
control the world supply of nutmeg and mace
build a naval base for war against China
find a route from Asia to the Pacific coast of Peru
questions.explanation: The Banda Islands were then the only source of nutmeg and mace. By seizing them, the VOC created a monopoly, run on plantations worked by enslaved and imported labour. It is a stark example of violence used for profit.

questions.stem: Olaudah Equiano's autobiography, published in London in 1789, describes his capture as a child in Africa and his experience of the Middle Passage. What makes it especially significant as a source?
options: It is an official record of every slave ship that sailed from Liverpool in the period
It was written by a plantation owner to explain how sugar was grown in Barbados
It gives the perspective of an enslaved person, and it was used to argue for abolition
It was written by a slave trader who wished to defend the trade to the British Parliament
questions.explanation: Equiano's narrative is one of the few accounts by a formerly enslaved African, and it was a powerful work in the British abolition campaign. Some historians debate details of his birthplace, but his account of slavery in the Atlantic world is valuable evidence.

questions.stem: Communities of people who escaped slavery, such as Palmares in Brazil and the Maroons of Jamaica, are significant because they show:
options: that the Portuguese Crown created reserves for freed Africans in Brazil
that slavery had ended in the Americas well before the eighteenth century
enslaved people's resistance by building free, self-governing communities
that planters freed their workers willingly once harvests were complete
questions.explanation: Maroon communities formed in remote areas, defended themselves and sometimes forced colonial governments to negotiate. Palmares lasted for most of the seventeenth century before it was destroyed in 1694.

questions.stem: In New Spain, the image of the Virgin of Guadalupe became a symbol of identity for many people born in the Americas. This shows:
options: the conversion of New Spain to Protestant Christianity
the rise of a colonial identity distinct from that of Spain
the end of Catholic belief in the Spanish American empire
the Spanish Crown's ban on religious images in its colonies
questions.explanation: Devotion to Guadalupe, associated with an apparition near Mexico City, grew into a symbol of a shared Mexican identity, combining Catholic faith with local pride. Such identities later fed independence movements.

questions.stem: Eighteenth-century ‘casta paintings’ from New Spain show families of mixed Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry, each labelled with a category. What do they best reveal?
options: Accurate census records showing exactly how many people lived in each of the categories
Indigenous artists' rejection of all Spanish ideas about race and social rank
That mixed marriages were forbidden in New Spain and punished by the Crown
An elite attempt to classify and rank people by ancestry in a mixed colonial society
questions.explanation: Casta paintings presented an ordered hierarchy of mixed ancestry, reflecting colonial elites' concern with status and ‘purity of blood’. They are representations, not reliable statistics, and show mixed families were common.

questions.stem: In 1755 the British expelled thousands of French-speaking Acadians from Nova Scotia. This expulsion is an example of:
options: the Acadians choosing to migrate to find better farmland
an imperial power removing a population it saw as disloyal
a peaceful exchange of settlers agreed in a treaty with France
a rebellion of settlers against heavy British taxation
questions.explanation: Fearing that Acadians would side with France, British authorities deported them, separating families and seizing their land. Many later settled in Louisiana, where their descendants became known as Cajuns.

questions.stem: The Seven Years' War (1756–1763) is often called the first global war because:
options: it lasted longer than any earlier war fought anywhere in the world
it was the first war fought with gunpowder weapons and artillery
it was fought in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa and India
it was the first war in which every European state fought on the same side
questions.explanation: Britain and France and their allies fought across several continents and oceans, including the war known in North America as the French and Indian War and the Battle of Plassey in India. Gunpowder had been in use for centuries.

questions.stem: Under the Treaty of Paris (1763), which ended the Seven Years' War, Spain recovered Havana, which Britain had captured in 1762. In return Spain gave Britain:
options: Florida
Louisiana
Gibraltar
the Philippines
questions.explanation: To recover Havana, Spain ceded Florida to Britain. Spain separately received Louisiana west of the river from France, Gibraltar had been British since 1713, and Britain returned Manila rather than gaining the Philippines.

questions.stem: After 1763, Britain passed the Stamp Act and other taxes on its American colonies. Which explanation best links the Seven Years' War to the American War of Independence?
options: Britain lost the war and handed the colonies to France, which provoked a revolt
The colonists wanted Britain to keep fighting France and resented the peace treaty
France forced the colonists to pay for the war after it had occupied the city of Boston
War debts led Britain to tax colonists, who rejected taxation without representation
questions.explanation: Britain won but faced huge debts and the cost of defending its expanded empire, so it taxed the colonies. Colonists argued that only their own assemblies could tax them, and protest turned to rebellion in 1775. Britain had won the war, not lost it.

questions.stem: From the British government's point of view, the main aim of the Royal Proclamation of 1763 was to:
options: punish the American colonists for smuggling and evading trade laws
open the western lands to settlers from French Quebec and Louisiana
avoid costly frontier wars by limiting settlement on Indigenous lands
raise revenue from the colonies to pay the debts of the Seven Years' War
questions.explanation: During Pontiac's War, Britain wanted to stabilise the frontier cheaply, so the Proclamation reserved land west of the Appalachians for Indigenous nations. It raised no revenue; taxes such as the Sugar and Stamp Acts were separate measures, though colonists' anger at the Proclamation line added to their grievances.

questions.stem: The revolution that began in the French colony of Saint-Domingue in 1791 is significant because it:
options: was a revolt of enslaved people that created the independent state of Haiti
was led by French planters who wanted the colony to join the United States
ended in the return of Saint-Domingue to Spain under the Treaty of Paris
was quickly crushed, so slavery continued in the colony until the 1880s
questions.explanation: Enslaved people rose against France's richest sugar colony; under leaders such as Toussaint Louverture they defeated French forces, and Haiti declared independence in 1804. It was the most successful slave revolt in history.

questions.stem: The dodo, a flightless bird found only on Mauritius, became extinct by the late seventeenth century after Dutch ships began visiting the island. This is an example of:
options: colonisation threatening native animals through hunting and introduced species
a disease carried to Europe by sailors returning from the Indian Ocean
the deliberate protection of native animals by the officials of the Dutch East India Company
a natural disaster that destroyed the island before Europeans ever arrived
questions.explanation: Sailors hunted dodos, and the rats, pigs and monkeys they introduced destroyed nests and eggs. The dodo became a symbol of extinction caused by human contact.

questions.stem: Clearing forests for sugar plantations on Caribbean islands such as Barbados most directly caused:
options: the return of Indigenous peoples to their traditional lands
the growth of new rainforests on the abandoned plantations
soil erosion and the loss of native forest and wildlife
a rise in rainfall that made the islands better for farming
questions.explanation: Barbados was almost completely cleared for sugar within decades of English settlement, leading to erosion, loss of habitat and dependence on imported timber and food. Environmental damage followed the drive for profit.

questions.stem: When the British established a penal colony at Sydney Cove in 1788, they claimed the land without any treaty with the Aboriginal peoples living there. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Britain acted as if no one owned the land, a view the High Court rejected in Mabo (1992)
Britain bought the land from the Eora people through a treaty signed by Governor Phillip
Britain left the land under Aboriginal law and settled only on unoccupied islands
Britain shared the land equally under a treaty that the colonial courts enforced
questions.explanation: The British acted as though the land belonged to no one, ignoring Aboriginal ownership and law. In Mabo v Queensland (No 2), the High Court rejected that doctrine, later called terra nullius, and recognised native title. Aboriginal peoples resisted dispossession, for example under Pemulwuy.

questions.stem: In 1793 Lord Macartney asked the Qianlong Emperor to open China to more British trade. The emperor replied that China possessed all things and had no need of British manufactures. This shows:
options: that Britain had promised to stop all trade with China after the mission
Qing confidence in China's self-sufficiency and its place at the centre of the world
that the Qing had already lost the Opium Wars and were being forced to refuse all trade
that China had no goods that the British wished to buy at the time
questions.explanation: Qianlong's reply expressed the tribute-system view of China as the centre of civilisation needing nothing from outside. Britain bought large amounts of Chinese tea; the trade imbalance later drove the opium trade and the Opium Wars of 1839–1842.

questions.stem: The Qing dynasty survived until 1911, but in the nineteenth century it lost wars to Britain, signed treaties that opened ports and gave up Hong Kong, and faced the Taiping Rebellion. Which judgement best describes Qing power in that century?
options: The dynasty continued, but its authority and independence were greatly reduced
The dynasty grew stronger, expanding its territory and closing all treaty ports
The dynasty was replaced by a British colonial government ruling all of China
The dynasty was unchanged, since none of these events affected its control
questions.explanation: The Qing kept the throne, but foreign powers gained privileges through the ‘unequal treaties’ and internal rebellions killed millions and weakened central control. This shows the balance of continuity and change in an empire's power.

questions.stem: Which legacy of the Portuguese Empire is still widely seen today?
options: Portuguese is the main language of India
Portuguese is the main language of Japan
Portuguese is the main language of Brazil
Portuguese is the main language of Mexico
questions.explanation: Brazil, Portugal's largest colony, became independent in 1822 but kept Portuguese as its language; it is now the country with the most Portuguese speakers. Mexico speaks Spanish, a legacy of the Spanish Empire.

questions.stem: Chillies, first grown in the Americas, became central to the cooking of India and Thailand. This is best explained as a legacy of:
options: Portuguese trade linking the Americas, Africa and Asia
Mughal conquests in the Americas in the sixteenth century
the Ming tribute missions sent across the Pacific Ocean
the overland Silk Road trade of the Han dynasty
questions.explanation: Portuguese ships carried American crops such as chillies to their Asian ports, including Goa, from where they spread rapidly. This is a lasting cultural legacy of the Columbian Exchange and empire. The Silk Road long predates contact with the Americas.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the British Empire's most lasting legacy in countries such as Australia, India and Canada is political. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Each still pays a yearly tax to the British Crown under the Navigation Acts
Each was granted independence on the same day by a single act of Parliament
Each has English as its only language, with no other languages spoken there
Each uses a parliamentary system and common law derived from British models
questions.explanation: Westminster-style parliaments and the common law are shared legacies of British rule. The Navigation Acts were repealed in the nineteenth century, independence came at different times and in different ways, and all three countries have many languages.
